courseEvidence.description2: Examines law from legal, socio‑scientific and normative perspectives. Explores definitions, legal traditions and fields of law, investigates the relationship between law and society and the concept of justice, and includes case law, excursion to international legal organisations, interviews with practitioners and a moot court session.
courseEvidence.name: Law, Society & Justice
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces law through legal, social and normative perspectives. Students compare major legal traditions and survey public and private law, including constitutional, criminal, international, human-rights, property, contract and tort law. The second part examines justice, social control and change, race and gender. Case briefs, legal interpretation, demand letters and mock trials apply legal reasoning; a family-law topic supports the design of a small socio-legal research proposal.

courseEvidence.description2: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
courseEvidence.name: Introduction to Sociology
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces sociological reasoning through classical theories, their historical settings and perspectives that address exclusions from the discipline. Students connect solidarity, modernity, identity, social boundaries, networks and stratification to race, gender, migration and inequality in education and work. A group paper develops a sociological question and analyzes a social problem using theory and academic literature.

courseEvidence.description2: Offers a legal, historical and philosophical approach to human rights. Studies classical and modern philosophers, traces the rise of human rights, examines the US Bill of Rights and the French Declaration, and discusses human rights treaties.
courseEvidence.name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
courseEvidence.profile: Studies human rights both as positive law and as philosophical claims. Students examine the UDHR, European and UN protection systems, monitoring institutions and landmark cases alongside natural law, natural rights, legal positivism and critiques of universality. Historical and philosophical texts frame debates about dignity, life and reproductive rights, punishment, religious freedom, expression and democracy. courseEvidence.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. courseEvidence.description2: Explores theories of moral reasoning—virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism—and discusses moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. courseEvidence.description2: Examines moral and legal justifications for criminalisation and punishment. It will equip you with the skills necessary to apply advanced statistical techniques to real-world research problems. courseEvidence.description2: Introduces political philosophy. Examines concepts such as authority, freedom, equality, democracy, human rights, pluralism, multiculturalism, poverty and environmental issues through classical and contemporary texts. Emphasises essay writing and presentations.

comparability: Criminal Law & Criminal Justice provides direct liability doctrine and a criminology proposal. Youth Resilience offers a concrete prevention intervention through educational practice. Psychology, developmental and clinical courses, law, social theory, and empirical methods support an interdisciplinary response. Media & Race adds analysis of crime and punishment representation. Histories of Gender adds actual historical sources and inquiry with incarceration as a bounded topic. General health assessment and international law do not supply forensic practice, domestic procedure or a crime-specific research capstone.

stoppingDecision.assessment: One qualified response is retained. Cybercrime is a genuine target interest, but general data analysis does not establish a digital-offending/investigation programme. The forensic minor concerns forensic psychiatry, legal psychology, penology, rehabilitation and forensic linguistics. The closest response already includes the available clinical, developmental and criminal-law contributions; a second forensic label would not yield a distinct supported 24-course curriculum. No third concept is considered after the second fails.
